The results obtained are then extended to a differential equation with a similar operator, and the evidence shows that the proof methods can yield unique solutions to the equation.

This work presents a study on solving polynomial linear systems with errors using an extension of the Berlekamp-Massey algorithm. It offers improved bounds on the number of iterations and matrix entries to solve such systems, especially in the case of small error probabilities. A new technique is also introduced to potentially terminate the algorithm early, which is proven to be effective in certain scenarios. Computational experiments are conducted to demonstrate the efficacy of these findings.

We propose a new phenomenon, parity-symmetry-protected bundle emission, which occurs when light interacts with a specific type of optical waveguide, known as a photonic "donut" or ring-shaped structure, that has a built-in symmetry defect. This interaction gives rise to higher-order light modes, or "light bundles," which are confined to specific areas and exhibit unique properties. Our research demonstrates that these light bundles can be emitted through a process involving a single photon, while maintaining a specific symmetry, thereby protecting the emission process and making it possible to control the light's behavior at the nanoscale.

A simplified analytical model is developed to describe the equilibrium properties of an alkali metal vapor, taking into account both dipole and quadrupole moments in an intuitive manner. The proposed model effectively captures the behavior of lower-energy states without requiring detailed quantum mechanical analysis. The accuracy of the model is verified through comparisons with both numerical simulations and existing quantum-based theories. The proposed model offers a more straightforward approach to calculating partition function components, enabling a closed-form expression for the free energy and related thermodynamic properties.

In the context of a medium with non-zero chiral condensate and imbalance, caused by real fermions' condensation, we investigate the vector spectral function. The medium's influence on the Dirac sea is represented through a dynamical fermion mass, which varies with momentum. The vector current's correlation function is calculated within a medium-modified Bethe-Salpeter equation framework. The results indicate that the medium's chiral imbalance induces radial splitting among vector mesons, in addition to existing longitudinal and transverse splitting components.

This paper presents an algorithm for estimating the size of an unknown network, assuming it follows a small-world model and that at least half of its nodes function correctly, with the remainder operating maliciously. The algorithm requires only a constant number of messages and a constant number number of message rounds, relying on a single port to send and receive data. It is designed for use on a ring network and operates within a distributed system without a central coordinator.

In numerical relativity, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints from the Einstein equations are resolved using an advanced initialization method called Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition. This approach decomposes the metric and anthon tensor into conformal and transverse-traceless components, which are determined by an operator applied to the twistless conformal metric. This decomposition is essential for avoiding singularities in numerical simulations. However, the conformal factor and the transverse-traceless variables must be found by solving the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints. This paper presents a new method called Conformal Transverse-Traceless with Krein, which uses an iterative process involving the Krein transformation to resolve these variables. This method is compared to other techniques such as the Bradley-Lake method and the Goldstein-Montoya method, and it outperforms them in a variety of test cases.

Our research involved mass testing a large quantity of 20-inch photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) for the JUNO neutrino experiment. A comprehensive evaluation of these PMTs was conducted at the BNL PMT lab using a customized 10-inch PMT tester, which allowed us to examine various aspects of the tubes' performance. A total of 82 20-inch PMTs were tested in a 2.5 liter water tank to simulate the neutrino detector's conditions. The test rig included a high voltage supply and a data acquisition system, which enabled us to collect relevant parameters such as anode response, pulse height distribution, and dark rate. The results showed that 97% of the tested PMTs met the required standards for the JUNO experiment.

Time series forecasting is a fundamental challenge with far-reaching applications in various fields. Recent advancements in using graph neural networks for time series prediction have shown promising results, particularly with the adaptive graph convolutional network (Adapt-GCN). This framework has several benefits, including its ability to learn correlations between different time series and their spatial displacements. The Adapt-GCN model has been successfully applied to three real-world problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in multidimensional time series prediction.

This research paper presents a detailed examination of the atmospheric dispersion models used in the initial study, focusing on the relationship between dispersion and alpha. The analysis includes an assessment of the models' accuracy and their correlation with the alpha parameter. The study also identifies the factors that influence the dispersion of light and establishes a relationship between dispersion and alpha for different atmospheric conditions. The findings of this research are then applied to develop a new equation for atmospheric dispersion that can be used in the analysis of high angular resolution data.

Recently, pre-trained models have become the preferred choice for solving
NLP tasks, but training these models is often prohibitively expensive due to
large required dataset sizes and costs. To mitigate this issue, knowledge
distillation can be employed by utilizing multiple teachers trained on labeled
data to produce reliable student models. In this research, a novel distillation
method called PILE is presented that uses an iterative logits calculation
approach to enhance distillation accuracy. PILE achieves state-of-the-art
results in 4 out of 6 datasets for labeled distillation tasks and also surpasses
the current best method in 3 unsupervised distillation tasks.

A potential alternative to the standard light dark matter model exists, where the dark matter particle has a very low mass. This model can be tested using a technique called intensity interferometry, which uses high-intensity laser pulses to detect non-gravitational, low-frequency interactions between dark matter particles. We have calculated the sensitivity of this method in detecting ultralight dark matter particles, taking into account the limitations imposed by thermal noise. Our findings indicate that high-power lasers and long detection distances are required to detect a 1 GeV/c^2 particle with a 10^-18 sensitivity level.

The basis pursuit in the continuum seeks the minimum-norm solution among a set of vector measures that represent a given load with a specific growth rate, resulting from a decomposition into a collection of closed, bounded regions with shared boundaries. Our study demonstrates that the solution is unique and involves a specific value of a variational energy that can be approximated numerically with confidence.

P4 has become the de facto standard for programming reconfigurable programmable switches. The VersaSwitch, a P4-based switch, allows direct P4 compilation with no translation required. The VSC compiler, a fully open-source compiler, supports P4-16 and P416 programs with a P416 compiler backend. The P416 compiler backend was introduced in 2019 but had limitations, including missing support for P416 features. The updated VSC compiler, version 20.04, includes a revised P416 compiler backend with support for P4-20 and P416 programs.

A crucial component in fluid dynamics is the vector transport equation, which determines the movement of a vector field within a flowing fluid. The equation's solution can be found using the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas finite elements, but the standard approach has a significant error (at least O(h^(-1)log(h))) when compared to the exact solution, especially in two-dimensional space. This study presents an improved method that significantly reduces the error (at least O(h^(-1))) for smooth initial conditions in two-dimensional space and O(h^(-1/2)) in three-dimensional space.

This study integrates decentralized machine learning techniques with fairness and privacy considerations. Specifically, it combines federated learning with fairness constraints and differential privacy, yielding novel formulations that balance communication efficiency with privacy and fairness. These formulations draw on the connection between fairness and kernel regression, allowing the derivation of optimal fairness and privacy trade-offs. Numerical examples demonstrate the relationship between fairness and privacy penalties and the communication costs associated with achieving them.

Researchers analyzing collision data from the LHCb experiment at various energy configurations discovered excited states of the $B_c^+$ meson. Specifically, two excited states were found with masses of around 6840 MeV and 6871 MeV, respectively. These findings also yielded corresponding width measurements of about 5.6 MeV and 6.2 MeV. The calculated mass and width values for the two-state system are consistent with predictions from LHCb's quark model analysis, which indicated the 6871 MeV state has a 0++ quantum state configuration.

This study introduces a type of Runge-Kutta method that can be extended to solve various types of differential equations, including those with variable coefficients and complex structures. The method is comprised of an infinite number of interconnected stages, each derived from a traditional Runge-Kutta formula. The study's initial focus is on continuous Runge-Kutta methods, specifically those based on the fourth-order Hermite polynomial, and it demonstrates that these methods can be effectively applied to solving differential problems in a simplified manner.

This paper introduces a novel, efficient algorithm called local critic training, enabling model-parallel learning of deep neural networks via transfer of gradients. The method overcomes the limitation of batch size imposed by the size of the parameter vector being updated. The proposed LTC method is comparable to the critic training used in Trust Region Policy Optimization, but with several key adaptations to suit model-parallel learning. The study demonstrates that LTC outperforms existing model-parallel deep learning methods and achieves comparable results to distributed SGD, with a significant improvement in communication efficiency.

We investigate how a non-uniform dissipation rate affects the Wada property in three-dimensional chaotic scattering. In a prior study, non-uniform dissipation was found to destroy the Wada property in two dimensions. In this study, introducing non-uniform dissipation in three dimensions leads to either destroying or enhancing the Wada property, depending on its value. When dissipation is lower than a certain critical value, the Wada property is preserved or even strengthened. We provide a theoretical explanation for these findings and the associated dynamics.

We investigate the possibility of light scalar or pseudoscalar particles that can change flavor but remain undetectable for an extended period. These flavor-changing neutral currents can be generated from various Higgs-like fields with accidental longevity, which result from global symmetries such as $U(1)N$ with $N=4,5,6$. The associated FCNC processes are particularly significant in the search for dark sectors using the phenomenon of lepton magnetic moment discrepancies.

This paper introduces a Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN), a novel architecture for action recognition in videos. The model leverages long-term spatial dependencies within individual frames and temporal dynamics across frames, achieved through the application of two hierarchical attention mechanisms. The first mechanism is applied to frame features, selecting the most relevant frames, while the second mechanism is applied to the temporal convolutional network (TCN) layers, amplifying the weight of less efficient layers to compensate for each other's weaknesses. The HAN is validated on two benchmark datasets, UCF101 and HMDB51, outperforming state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy and parameter efficiency.

The thermodynamic stability of Reissner-Nordstrom anti-de Sitter black holes under an external scalar field influence is investigated. Focusing on the thermodynamic phase transition and an analysis of the thermodynamic stability, it is found that the first-order phase transition is confirmed and the thermodynamic stability of the system is discussed using the criteria of conformal coupling and minimal coupling. Additionally, the study supports the weak cosmic censorship conjecture in the case of conformal coupling, but not in the case of minimal coupling.

The majestic beauty of star formation has captivated human imagination for centuries, yet its underlying processes are still complex and poorly understood. Researchers have made significant progress in deciphering the mysteries of star birth, thanks to an array of observational methods and high-performance computational tools. This article provides an overview of our present understanding of star formation, drawing from a wide range of studies, and highlights the most compelling evidence gathered through various techniques.

This paper introduces a new method for estimating uncertainty and relevance metrics, such as Shannon entropy and mutual information, in complex probability distributions that can be approximated using Nested Sampling. The method utilizes the samples and weights generated by an NS algorithm to calculate these entropies at any stage of the sampling process. The paper also provides a general framework for the computation of functional values of probability distributions, which is then applied to derive entropy estimation formulas. The method is then evaluated on various scenarios, including a simple analytical distribution, a 1D kinetic Monte Carlo model, a 2D energy landscape with multiple basins, and a multi-dimensional protein folding model simulated with Rosetta. The results show that the NS-based entropy estimates are highly accurate and reliable, even when the sampling process is still in progress.

We re-examine the conservation law $u_t + f(u)_t + (A(u))_x = 0$ with dissipation term $((A(u))_x)_t + (u_x)^2_x = 0$, focusing on a measure that is a combination of a continuous function and a Cantor measure. This analysis builds on previous work by Bressan and Han, which considered a related problem with a specific, more restricted measure. We introduce a new class of measures, called Type-1 measures, which include the combination of a continuous function and a Cantor measure, as well as the space of all Cantor measures. We define a weak solution using the concept of a signed Radon measure and establish the existence of a weak solution when the initial data consists of a Type-1 measure.

This research introduces NBcoded, a lightweight classification tool designed to
identify network attacks on resource-constrained devices. NBcoded utilizes
feature-engineering techniques to extract meaningful information from network
traffic data, which is then analyzed through a two-stage process involving
Naive Bayes and Encoder models. The former captures complex patterns in the
data, while the latter, a linear model, provides a precise classification of
network incidents. The study showcases NBcoded's effectiveness on three real-
world network intrusion datasets, highlighting its ability to run efficiently on
low-resource devices without compromising accuracy.

For a finite group G, the problem of growing actions involves determining whether there are actions of G on a sequence of distinct sets that result in increasing action sizes. We resolve this problem for solvable groups of arbitrary order by providing two distinct proofs. One proof leverages the fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups, while the other utilizes the nilpotency of solvable groups.

This research focuses on using computer technology to identify living organisms moving in recorded footage. A novel algorithm is developed to recognize and track these organisms, which can be found in various environments, such as underwater or in terrestrial settings. The algorithm is tested using a diverse dataset of videos featuring different types of movement, including crawling, slithering, walking, and swimming. The results show that it can accurately detect and distinguish between these forms of movement with high precision, especially when the organisms are moving at a slow pace.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimizing surplus generation to minimize costs, a task that can be achieved through solving the Bilevel Optimal Power Flow (B-OPF) problem. B-OPF is a complex optimization challenge, with two nested optimization issues that represent the strategies of generators and transmission system operators. We present a quantum approach to tackling B-OPF by utilizing a mixed quantum-classical hybrid method, combining the quantum simulation of B-OPF's lower-level problem on a special machine and classical optimization techniques. Our hybrid method is compared to a purely classical solution that applies the Benders decomposition method, showing significant time savings in finding a solution.

The pursuit of fundamental physical laws is a longstanding objective, yet the increasing complexity of modern experimental techniques is creating a significant disparity between theoretical and experimental physics. We can reduce this discrepancy by employing machine learning algorithms that can identify universal physical laws from empirical data without prior assumptions. This paper explores the potential of such an approach, highlighting both the successes and challenges of using machine learning to discover physical laws.

This study utilizes the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data. The search targets particles with large ionising power, resulting in a slowed-down velocity or heavy mass. The study focuses on long-lived particles that interact with the detector for an adequate amount of time, allowing for a minimum detection distance of 1 millimeter. The data is compared to the standard model predictions for real and simulated events, including the signatures of $Z^\prime$ and $T$ boson decays, as well as the results of the searches for charginos and gluinos, decaying to electrons or photons. The study sets new limits on the cross-section for the production of these particles at various mass and lifetime combinations, with some limits reaching as high as 1 femtobarn for the $Z^\prime$ boson in the mass range of 200-300 GeV, assuming a 2-10 millimeter decay length.

We have developed a technique to enhance the photon collection efficiency of on-chip single-photon sources based on quantum dots by using ridge waveguides. This design minimizes the mismatch between the quantum dot and waveguide modes, resulting in a theoretical efficiency of 99.7%. Our experiments using a sample grown by molecular beam epitaxy have shown an overall photon collection efficiency of 97.7% across multiple quantum dots. This has resulted in a 65% increase in the probability of a single quantum dot emitting a photon per attempt. This improvement will lead to more efficient on-chip single-photon source systems.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool for studying the boson peak, a vibrational state near the lightest sound wave velocity in glassy systems. The boson peak is characterized by a highly dispersed state with varying frequencies across different materials, which can be effectively explored using inelastic neutron scattering. The technique allows researchers to analyze the boson peak's dynamics and anharmonicity in glass-forming substances, as evidenced by our previous studies on PDCPD PEG and PEG. The anharmonic nature of the boson peak is reflected in the dispersion of the density of states and the vibrational state's width, both of which can be measured through inelastic neutron scattering.

This article presents a thorough examination of the two-loop Feynman integrals that arise in the calculation of the Higgs decay rate to gamma-gamma, involving massive top and bottom quarks and a massive W boson. These integrals feature a range of distinctive numerators and five distinct kinematic configurations, leading to a total of 41 master integrals that cannot be simplified further. Our analysis employs novel integration techniques to derive exact closed-form solutions for all 41 master integrals.

In random systems, a unique set of high-conductance channels exists that allow energy to be transmitted with minimal loss. These channels, known as "eigenchannels," can be established and calculated using a technique that involves analyzing a system's "optical" properties. Two key formulas, sum rules, emerge in this context, which help to understand the eigenchannels' properties and ensure they meet specific requirements. Notably, these channels must exist in both the forward and reverse directions of energy transmission. Building on previous research, this study expands our understanding of these channels in scattering systems by developing new theoretical frameworks for calculating their conductance and phase. These frameworks lead to the derivation of two key sum rules, which are then validated through numerical simulations in two different scenarios.

Researchers have identified a new spiral arm in the Milky Way galaxy, which they're calling the far 3-Kpc arm. This finding was made possible by a detailed analysis of molecular gas data, which revealed a previously unknown feature extending from the Central Molecular Zone to a radial distance of around 2.5 parsecs. The far 3-Kpc arm appears to be a continuous structure composed of molecular gas, and its mass is estimated to be approximately 5.5 million solar masses. The far 3-Kpc arm is thought to have formed around 10 million years ago as a result of a gas inflow, which was triggered by a bar-like structure in the galaxy's center. The far 3-Kpc arm is now being studied to determine its impact on the galaxy's chemical composition and its role in the formation of new stars.

Our study examines how different optimization algorithms generate diverse solutions during the search process, beyond finding multiple optima. We use a range of benchmark functions and varied population sizes in multi-objective optimization to compare various single-objective and multi-objective algorithms. Our analysis reveals that even single-objective algorithms can outperform multi-objective versions in creating diverse populations, contradicting common assumptions. By conducting a comprehensive trade-off surface analysis, we gain insights into the diversity of solutions and how it affects the population's distribution.

The Stable Roommates problem involves a group of distinct individuals who need to be paired in romantic relationships in such a way that no single person would prefer another as a match. A more complex version of this problem, known as the Stable Roommates problem with preferences that can be broken down, has been studied extensively. In this paper, we explore a three-dimensional form of this problem, where each person's preferences can be quantified using numerical values in a specific format, and we show that finding a stable matching in this scenario is an NP-complete problem even when the input data is restricted to a specific format. However, we also identify specific conditions under which finding a stable matching becomes a more complex problem, and propose an algorithm that can provide good matches under certain constraints in a reasonable amount of time.

In two-dimensional materials with a flat valley structure, the interaction between electrons and phonons plays a crucial role in their overall properties. Traditionally, the electron-phonon coupling mechanism is understood to arise from the deformation potential, which is influenced by the movement of atoms. However, in systems with strong interatomic bonds, the release of energy during deformation can lead to the creation of new interatomic coupling mechanisms, which are proportional to the interatomic distance. These novel coupling mechanisms can significantly affect the curvature of the electronic bands and the work function, and have the potential to impact valley transport and other related phenomena.

The concept of $\varepsilon$-nets and the Gromov-Hausdorff distance play a crucial role in modern metric geometry. This distance measures the minimum distortion required when deforming two metric spaces into each other. A key class of metric spaces that achieve this minimal distortion are the $\varepsilon$-clouds, which are obtained by taking the images of all possible $\varepsilon$-nets from one space onto another under optimal deformations. This paper proves that these $\varepsilon$-clouds possess a unique center, which can be found by taking the average of all possible $\varepsilon$-nets, and shows that this center is stable in the sense that it remains the same even if the distance $\varepsilon$ is slightly changed. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that these $\varepsilon$-clouds are complete in the sense that they have no "holes" or "gaps" in them, which is an important property that ensures the existence of a unique center.

This research proposes a microstrip patch antenna operating at mm-waves with an expanded bandwidth of 4.2 GHz and a broad angular coverage of 72 degrees. Designed using the widely-used Rogers substrate, the antenna exhibits a high level of stability across different environments without significant changes in its reflection coefficient or broadside radiation pattern. The simulated results indicate an end-fire radiation pattern with minimal variation within the specified bandwidth. The antenna's broad angular coverage and stable performance make it suitable for various applications, including communication systems and sensors, while its planar microstrip configuration facilitates easy integration into mm-wave systems.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code. Despite being simple, these codes require efficient decoders to function reliably. Traditional decoders used in such codes were based on belief propagation, but this approach has limitations, especially in the face of complex errors. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of neural network decoders, but these require vast amounts of data and are challenging to modify. This study presents a reinforcement learning method for generating efficient decoding policies without the need for extensive data sets. The learned policies outperform traditional approaches in various scenarios.

We investigate the quantum jump metrology in an optomechanal two-cavity network, where a quantum Erbium-doped fiber amplifier photon serves as the initial standard. Our analysis reveals that the precision of the optical phase measurement can be improved by utilizing the quantum jumps of the mechanical oscillators and the light fields within the cavity. This enhancement is specifically demonstrated in the Hamming bound limit, where the optimal precision achieves a significant improvement of $\sqrt{N}$, rather than the usual $\sqrt{2N}$ precision limit.

The PHENIX Collaboration has measured correlations between direct photons and hadrons in Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions at RHIC. These correlations were examined at various points in rapidity and were found to be altered in Au$+$Au collisions at high transverse momentum, indicating interactions between jets and the medium. In contrast, $d$$+$Au collisions showed no significant changes, suggesting these effects are confined to heavy-ion collisions.

We propose a hybrid digital-analog approach to simulating fermionic systems on a quantum computer. This method leverages the capabilities of analog quantum computers in generating complex wavefunctions while leveraging digital quantum computers' ability to perform precise operations. By combining these features, we can efficiently run Fermi-Hubbard simulations and study complex phenomena like quantum phase transitions.

Deep neural networks are highly effective due to their capacity for complex model representation. However, achieving optimal generalization performance also depends on optimizing the model, as over-parameterization can lead to poor generalization. This study investigates the interplay between model complexity and optimization to address the optimization-generalization dilemma. We introduce a novel approach that enhances feature construction to improve generalization. The proposed method, based on the feature alignment of layer-wise representations, outperforms existing techniques and demonstrates a straightforward implementation that integrates seamlessly into the standard training process.

A novel approach to creating a light control system utilizes a field-programmable gate array to manage a spatial light modulator, enabling rapid and efficient propagation of light waves that conform to predetermined light distribution patterns. This proprietary method enables the formation of multiple complex three-dimensional structures within a single medium, even when the light is scattered. To validate its effectiveness, experiments were conducted using a light with a wavelength of 633 nanometers and various numerical aperture values, achieving successful transmission of light through the medium, resulting in the formation of the desired structures.

We appreciate the valuable comments and suggestions provided by the discussants. 
Chang, Zhao, and Li note that our work's assumptions might be too stringent and 
consider alternative approaches that relax these conditions. They recommend using 
high-order Taylor expansions to approximate the Q-function, which could improve 
efficiency but also introduces bias. We agree that exploring such approximations 
is a worthwhile direction for future research. 
Li and Zhao also mention that our method's computational cost may be high due to 
the need to solve QP problems. They suggest leveraging problem sparsity or using 
stochastic gradient descent for optimization in large-scale applications. We agree 
that reducing computational complexity is crucial for practical applications and 
welcome further discussions on this aspect.

Monolithic small collection-electrode technology has emerged as a promising direction for future Large Hadron Collider experiments. The CLICTD design, a small collection-electroide, was developed to test this concept and is being studied by the CMS collaboration. The CLICTD was built using different sensor materials, 25 um thick LGSO, 300 um thick LGSO, and 250 um thick CMOS, all on various substrates, including HV-CMOS, epitaxial float zone, and p-type ingots. The study examined the performance of each sensor, focusing on its charge collection properties, position resolution, and response to magnetic fields. The results showed that the 25 um LGSO sensor exhibited the best performance, with a position resolution of 700 um, while the 300 um LGSO sensor had a position resolution of 900 um. The 250 um CMOS sensor demonstrated a position resolution of 800 um. The study's findings are crucial for guiding the development of CLICTD modules and monolithic detectors.

A new method has been successfully tested on a real-world system for the first time, allowing it to effectively remove turbulence from an image in mid-air. This method uses an adaptive optics system that uses a camera to capture speckles in real-time and uses the image itself to correct the wavefront, resulting in high-quality image restoration. Experiments were conducted under severe atmospheric conditions using a high-speed adaptive optics system with a high frame rate, and the results show that this method can provide high-quality image restoration even in the most challenging conditions.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to address negative interest rates in a specific bond pricing context, building upon the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross formula. We introduce a new model, the deterministic-shift CIR model, which modifies the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross formula by incorporating a constant adjustment to the yield curve equation. We then derive the partial average variance-adjustment method, a numerical solution approach, and examine the behavior of the model's ergodic distribution. The deterministic-shift CIR model is compared to two alternative solutions, the extended CIR model and the Hull-White model, in terms of calibration metrics.

Long-standing discrepancies within the solar model have prompted the hypothesis of neutrino oscillations into hidden states.
The DUNE experiment, with its wide energy range and high statistics, holds significant potential in investigating these sterile neutrinos.
By utilizing solar neutrinos as LNS (long neutrino source) beams, we can establish two distinct areas of interest: 
the low-energy region, which can be studied with a segmented water detector, and the high-energy region, which requires a more detailed examination.
Our analysis suggests that DUNE has a substantial potential in confirming the existence of 1 eV sterile neutrinos, with a comparable sensitivity to SOLARMAX with a 3-water-SD detector in the low-energy region and with a 20-kt liquid-argon detector in the high-energy region.

Meta-analyses that incorporate the influence of covariates on treatment size are known as meta-regressions. When dealing with the treatment of binary outcomes, a meta-regression model that accounts for the correlation within a study is referred to as a cluster-correlated meta-regression. This paper presents three new cluster-correlated meta-regression models that take into consideration the bivariate treatment of outcomes, as well as the influence of covariates. These models are based on two different assumptions regarding the residual structure, namely that the residuals are either multivariate normal or a specific type of matrix-normal. We derive the asymptotic distribution of the proposed estimators, and present a simulation that demonstrates their performance under different data conditions. Finally, the proposed estimators are applied to a real-world dataset.

A novel integration algorithm for particle collision in discrete element method simulations has been developed, allowing for multiple time steps per finite element volume. Unlike existing methods that use a fixed collision time, this new algorithm uses a variable time step that's based on the average velocity of colliding particles and their relative velocity. This approach eliminates the need for a minimum time step, making it more efficient than standard discrete element method simulations. A new formula for calculating the collision count and normal vector has also been introduced, enabling the simulation of complex particle collisions without interference from other particles. This method has been successfully tested in two scenarios: a single particle colliding with a stationary wall and two particles colliding in a head-on collision.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has led to a hypothesis that particle creation is driven by fluctuations in the gravitational field rather than antipodal vacuum fluctuations. To test this, we examined the gravitational field's fluctuation impact on a massless scalar field in global spacetime, finding that these fluctuations can indeed give rise to scalar field pairs. The total energy of these pairs originates from the gravitational field's energy release. The Unruh/Hawking process can be reinterpreted as a manifestation of gravitational field radiation due to a black hole's emergence.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on nuclear parton distribution functions and its impact on nuclear structure functions at the LHC regime are investigated using a color dipole approach. This approach allows for a calculation of the transverse momentum broadening of partons in cold nuclear matter, which in turn influences the parton model description of nuclear structure functions. It is found that transverse momentum broadening significantly affects the parton model description of nuclear structure functions, particularly at large-x and high-Q^2 conditions, and that this effect is more pronounced in the case of longitudinal structure functions.
This article presents a comprehensive set of distinct integer solution pairs $(a, b)$ for the equation $a^2 + ab + b^2 = 7^n$, valid for all positive integer values of $n$.

The interaction between a liquid jet and a surrounding stream flow is analyzed within a channel context. The resulting instability is examined through both two-dimensional and three-dimensional simulations, considering the effects of different parameters such as jet velocity, stream velocity, and surface tension on the jet's penetration into the stream. The study employs the Volume of Fluids method to model the liquid phase and assumes a perfect gas for the stream phase, with the stream velocity and density represented by average values. The simulations reveal that a stable liquid jet can develop a penetration mode similar to a classical Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, influenced by the relative velocities of the jet and stream, and affected by surface tension, especially in three-dimensional scenarios.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on memory that can withstand crashes, but the rising cost of such memory is a significant barrier to entry. To overcome this, we propose an innovative approach that ensures the reliability of volatile main memory by leveraging the characteristics of non-volatile memory to recover from crashes in advanced systems. Our method focuses on linear data structures used in algorithms, such as stacks and queues, and allows for seamless crash recovery through the following mechanisms. First, we maintain a checkpoint of the data structure's state at regular algorithm progress milestones. Second, we identify and manage conflicts that arise from multiple threads accessing the same data structure. Third, we handle the insertion and deletion of elements during crash recovery. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to various algorithms that employ linear data structures, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through a real-world example using the Okami search algorithm.

The internet and social media are exemplars of complex information networks that require effective organization into manageable structures, known as hierarchies, for comprehensive comprehension. In this context, we introduce two scalable models for computing these hierarchies: the MDH Model and the TDH Model, which leverage a combination of depth and temporal characteristics to inform their architecture. Our proposed models aim to address the limitations of existing methods, such as the RFH Model, by efficiently computing and representing these hierarchies within a real-time framework. Our approach enables the computation of 1,000,000 nodes in just 12.7 seconds using 8 cores, outperforming the RFH Model's performance by a factor of 3.

We examine the validity of a statistical model that estimates the probability of escape for three-body gravitational systems as a function of the initial total energy of the system. This model is based on the properties of granular materials and was previously tested on the three-body problem with equal-mass particles in a planar setup. In this study, we expand the scope by considering a range of non-planar configurations and initial conditions that violate the assumptions of the statistical model. We discover that its predictions are accurate for a substantial range of energies, but less precise in scenarios that involve large angular velocities or initial conditions with high potential energy.

The ALICE experiment has investigated the suppression of the $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ mesons in PbPb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The study focused on prompt and nonprompt charmonium production in the most central collisions. The $J/\psi$ was found to be more heavily suppressed than $\psi(2S)$, with both suppression levels increasing with collision centrality. The observed suppression of $J/\psi$ is in line with expectations based on a model that attributes the effect to the influence of the quark-gluon plasma. The suppression of $\psi(2S)$, however, is more pronounced than predicted by the same model, suggesting additional factors at play.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's semantics can be interpreted within a hyperdoctrine-based
topos framework. This hyperdoctrine is essentially a generalized version of
the hyperdoctrine described in [Blok and van Alten 2000]. We demonstrate that
the proposed hyperdoctrine is consistent with the established framework of
continuous logic, as described in [Ben-Yosef and Hodkinson 2013 and Ben-Yosef
2015]. Furthermore, we show that the hyperdoctrine's category of predicates
forms a topos, with the associated sheaf topology being the locale topology
derived from the space of formulas.

The development of software systems has become a complex process, and ensuring their high quality is essential. Test cases play a crucial role in this process, and choosing the right ones is vital to save time and resources. The test case selection algorithm based on singular value decomposition is an effective method for this purpose, and this study aims to improve its efficiency by parallelizing it using the MPI protocol, taking into account the scalability of different architectures.

This research paper introduces a novel deep sequential model that combines information from clinical interviews and text-based data to predict suicidal ideation in patients. It proposes a framework for addressing the inherent time complexities in both data types by utilizing a specific type of recurrent neural network. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through an application in a dataset containing suicidal ideation data from 615 patients, showing its ability to accurately identify time frames when suicidal ideation occurs. The model achieved a high level of performance, with an AUC of 0.85 for clinical data and 0.83 for text data, outperforming a baseline model that combined the two data types.

The supernova remnant Cassiopeia A is one of the most intense sources of hard X-rays in the sky, resulting from the interaction of a massive star's explosion with its surrounding interstellar space. The X-ray emission from this remnant is primarily produced by two elements: nickel, which has a half-life of approximately 5 days and is a direct byproduct of the supernova, and cobalt, which has a half-life of about 3.8 years and is created from nickel through radioactive decay. The X-ray light curves of these elements are distinct, with nickel exhibiting a steady decrease in intensity over time and cobalt displaying a more complex, irregular pattern. The X-ray polarization of Cassiopeia A has been studied in the past using the Chandra and XMM-Newton satellites, yielding a polarized intensity of about 10% in the 2-10 keV energy range. The IXPE mission, launched in 2019, has now successfully measured the X-ray polarization of Cassiopeia A at higher energy levels, achieving a precision of about 5%. The observed polarization of 4.6% ± 1.2% at 6-10 keV is consistent with the predictions of 3.9% ± 0.8% based on the combination of nickel and cobalt emissions. The IXPE results are in line with the idea that both the forward and reverse shocks produced in the supernova explosion contribute to the observed

The problem of finding the minimum number n of nonnegative integers for which the sum of any two differs by a square has been a longstanding Diophantine problem. In this paper, we explore several variations of this problem, including one where the sums are bounded by a given number M, and thetas, the angles of the triangle formed by the points (k, l, k+l), lie within a specified range.

The characteristics of dense stellar matter are influenced by various factors, including the presence of strange quarks and dense nuclear matter. In this study, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the sound velocity in dense matter composed of quarks and nuclear matter, using a specific equation of state that incorporates the Walecka model for nuclear interactions and the MIT bag model for quarks. We also consider the effects of different vector meson exchanges in nuclear interactions on sound velocity. Our findings on sound velocity are used to investigate the adiabatic index in dense matter and its implications for the properties of compact stars, such as their mass-radius relations and gravitational redshift.

We investigate a set of quantum states known as "compass states," which are generated through the interaction of two modes in an optical field via a parametric process. These states exhibit unique properties in the Fock space, and our analysis shows how varying one mode's squeezing and displacement affects these properties. By applying a parametric transformation, we map the properties of the compass states onto a 2D grid, allowing us to identify the characteristics of both modes. We also demonstrate how to generate compass states experimentally using a nonlinear optical cavity.

This study introduces a novel method to analyze the intricate structures formed in two-dimensional multiphase flows by tracking the boundaries between different phases.
The proposed approach utilizes a skeleton representation of these interfaces to capture their geometric properties and thereby distinguish between different morphologies, such as droplets, bubbles, and jets, which exhibit distinct topological characteristics. A comparison with existing methods on real-world data reveals that the proposed technique outperforms others in identifying these complex interfaces.

Certain enveloped viruses exhibit active movement on the surfaces of host cells by rolling in a spiral pattern. This motility facilitates their invasion into cellular membranes, but a specific mechanism has yet to be identified. We've developed a theoretical framework to investigate their movement and observed that a spiral shape provides the necessary stability for propulsive forces to function. Furthermore, a motor-based model and a flexural tile model have been proposed to explain the self-rolling motion of these viruses.

We've conducted a comprehensive study of S0 galaxies within a specific Hubble type range in the SDSS dataset and found that U-type warps are more prevalent in galaxy clusters. This research reveals that the probability of a galaxy having a U-type warp is directly correlated with its velocity dispersion within the cluster, and is most pronounced in clusters exceeding 500 km/s velocity dispersion. This relationship is most evident for galaxies classified as S0/a to S0.2H galaxies. Furthermore, we've identified a correlation between the probability of a U-type warp and the galaxy's concentration index, with more concentrated galaxies being more likely to exhibit U-type warps. This pattern holds true across all Hubble types within the selected range. We've also found that the majority of jellyfish galaxies in the SDSS dataset align with the U-type warp category, and that their U-type warp probability peaks at a higher concentration index compared to field galaxies, yet at a lower concentration index compared to jellyfish galaxies exhibiting U-type warps. This suggests that the U-type warp stage in jellyfish galaxies corresponds to a less concentrated state.

This study demonstrates a distinct Liouville theorem for convex Ricci shrinkers with constant scalar curvature.
In addition, it offers an alternative proof for L. Zhang's Liouville theorem, focusing on convex Ricci shrinkers with non-negative curvature.
The investigation also establishes a distinct implication of a recent discovery by J. Wang and Y. Wang regarding convex Ricci shrinkers with constant scalar curvature.

We have discovered the presence of chirality in phonon modes in cubic $A$Bi$_{2}$ ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) materials with a Laves phase structure. The investigation involved a first-principles calculation within the framework of the harmonic approximation. The study revealed that the chiral phonon modes are protected by symmetry and occur in the Brillouin zone center. The protected nature of these modes is due to the breaking of spatial inversion symmetry and the presence of time reversal symmetry. The existence of these chiral phonon modes is a result of the materials' lack of inversion symmetry in their crystal structure.

The Born effective charge is a key concept in the study of phonons, dielectric properties, and the polar interaction between electrons. This work extends the definition of the Born effective charge to nonadiabatic conditions and calculates it for several metals, demonstrating that its real part is finite at zero frequency. A crucial connection between the Born effective charge and the Drude weight is established, which is also verified by explicit numerical calculations in the case of lead.

We investigate the impact of thermal fluctuations on incompressible fluid turbulence, focusing on the interplay between the thermal energy and kinetic energy of the fluid. Our analysis reveals that thermal fluctuations significantly influence the energy cascade in turbulent flows, particularly in the dissipation range where the interactions between eddies and viscosity play a crucial role. The results of our study suggest that the turbulence cascade is not entirely self-similar when thermal fluctuations are taken into account, leading to a non-zero intercept in the resulting Kolmogorov spectrum. The influence of thermal fluctuations is more pronounced in the dissipation range than the inertial range, with the former exhibiting a thermal energy spectrum that is directly proportional to the wavenumber and viscosity, and inversely proportional to the thermal energy. The implications of our findings are particularly relevant to the context of fluid turbulence in the presence of solid boundaries, where the dissipation range is significantly altered due to the interaction with boundaries.

A new phenomenon, referred to as the topological magnetoelectric effect, is proposed. It arises from a time-reversal invariant non-linear response that is observable in three-dimensional topological insulators with band structures characterized by half-integer quantum Hall properties. The effectiveness of the time-reversal symmetry is illustrated through the modulation of a surface current under the influence of an external magnetic field, as well as the Witten effect, where a magnetic monopole's presence causes a three-dimensional topological insulator to develop a finite electric charge.

In a two-dimensional delay system with a non-linear interaction between its components, we observe chaotic diffusion that is significantly amplified when one of its parameters is periodically modulated. This modulation, which affects the delay time, leads to a substantial enhancement of the chaotic diffusion by several orders of magnitude, depending on its frequency and amplitude. By analyzing the system's stochastic dynamics, we find that its transport properties are closely related to a delay version of the standard map, which exhibits an increased scaling factor for diffusion when the delay time is modulated. This increase is the primary reason for the significant enhancement of the chaotic diffusion.

We establish a rigorous semantics for the stochastic lambda calculus by adapting a domain-theoretic approach previously used for the probabilistic lambda calculus. The resulting semantics effectively captures the intended meaning of the stochastic lambda calculus. To demonstrate the utility of this semantics, we show that the semantics of closed terms is equivalent to a fixed point of a continuous function in a topological space, and we identify a specific topology that corresponds to the semantics.

In software design, conclusions drawn from discussions about code are typically considered final and not subject to further discussion. This property of software design conclusions being uncontestable is leveraged to develop a conclusion stability metric for discussion threads, which measures the extent to which participants agree on a conclusion. This stability metric in turn is used to create an indicator of uncontestable conclusions within software design documentation, which is found to be more consistently agreed upon by developers compared to indicators based on general text patterns.

This paper proposes a groundbreaking explanation for the origin of gravity, suggesting it arises from a coherent vacuum field that can traverse through time in the reverse direction following the inflation era. The concept is based on the principles of quantum mechanics applied to the universe as a whole, where the coherent nature of the gravitational field allows it to span across space and move backwards in time. The idea is further supported by the fact that quantum mechanics exhibits non-locality and entanglement, as well as the Coherent Holographic Vacuum (CHV) model, which has been successful in predicting various phenomena observed in high-energy particle physics. The CHV model is seen as an extension of the macro-quantum coherence paradigm, where the coherence of matter and gravitational fields is not limited to the microscopic scale, but rather can be present on a cosmological scale.

Proximal methods can be used to optimize a variety of non-convex objectives by mapping the domain to a convex framework, but the proximal gradient method struggles to identify the underlying manifold it's projecting onto, especially in high-dimensional spaces. By analyzing its behavior, we show that the proximal gradient method generates a sequence of iterates that converge to a point on the manifold, and we develop a new scheme, based on Newton's method, that converges to a minimum on the manifold, even in high dimensions.

This paper provides a detailed examination of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals in commutative rings, along with their equivalent forms and distinctive characteristics. Further, it identifies the type of ideal domains in which every prime ideal is a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal.

The analysis utilized a 287.6 $	ext{fb}^{-1}$ dataset collected from the Belle II experiment, utilizing a novel approach that identified the recoil $B$ meson through hadronic decays. u_\ell$ decays. The signal was isolated by exploiting kinematic differences and cross-checked with a separate approach that directly reconstructed the $ho$ resonance. The resulting upper limit on branching ratio for $B^+ 	o ho^+ \ell

Spectroscopy is a fundamental tool for exploring the universe, and a newer variant, cross-correlation spectroscopy, has been gaining traction in astrophotonic applications. This technique offers several benefits over traditional methods, such as enhanced sensitivity, a broader wavelength range, and the ability to process multiple signals simultaneously. However, it also presents unique challenges in terms of fiber optics and photonic devices. This paper delves into the latest advancements in using these devices for spectroscopic analysis and discusses their current limitations and potential future developments.

In recent years, machine learning has become a key component in drug development, 
particularly in the area of drug repurposing where a pre-approved drug's potential 
analogues are identified. This process involves predicting a drug's similarity to 
another based on molecular structure, and various models have been developed to achieve 
this through either graph-based methods or attention-mechanism enabled neural networks.
However, these models are often presented in isolation, lacking a broader comparison 
with other approaches. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive review of existing 
methods, and performed a unified evaluation of these techniques on available datasets.

This paper introduces a pioneering approach to road damage identification, enabling effective transfer of knowledge from one region to another, taking into account varying lighting conditions. Traditional methods of automatic road damage detection are limited by their inability to adapt to different environments, a major shortcoming. To overcome this, we have developed a sophisticated framework that can learn from images of one area and apply that knowledge to identify issues in another. Our results demonstrate the ability of this framework to detect damage in Japanese roads using data from the UK and Japan as the base for learning.

Imitation learning effectively transfers skills across domains when the action space is linear, by leveraging a general representation that maps observations to actions within multiple environments. However, this approach is limited to A^ℝ^d action spaces, where imitation learning can be shown to optimize a maximum likelihood objective. We demonstrate that this framework still yields beneficial results, even in more complex action spaces, by applying it to a dataset of real-world robotic observations.

The initial stages of a Population III star's formation are heavily influenced by its surrounding protostellar disk, which forms through gas accretion. A study by Machida et al. revealed that a massive magnetic field amplification occurs near the Population III star protostar, significantly affecting the disk's formation. This amplification is caused by the rapid growth of the mean-field dynamo and the development of a toroidal magnetic field. As a result, the disk's inner region is heavily influenced by the strong magnetic flux, which leads to the formation of a magnetized accretion disk. This phenomenon has a substantial impact on the gas accretion rate and the protostar's mass growth rate. Furthermore, the intense magnetic field prevents the growth of the disk's radial width and the development of gravitational instability, which in turn hinders the formation of planetary-mass objects.

Association rule analysis involves data mining tasks such as generating association rules, identifying essential deduction schemes, and constructing minimal association rule bases. Our study focuses on two types of redundancy in association rules - horizontal and vertical redundancy - and shows that removing either form of redundancy leads to the same association rule base. We also introduce a new, polynomial-time algorithm for removing horizontal redundancy and two new, linear-time algorithm for removing vertical redundancy, both of which construct the minimum-size association rule base. Furthermore, we establish a connection between horizontal and vertical redundancy and certain association rule deducibility properties, and introduce new, efficient deduction schemes based on this relationship.

This research investigates the impact of court-ordered psychotherapy on convicted offenders' mental health, specifically focusing on those with severe personality disorders. Using a dataset from the UK's Ministry of Justice, we examine how receiving this therapy affects offenders' mental health over time, in comparison to those who do not receive the order. We consider several factors that might influence the decision to impose the order, including the offender's age and prior convictions, and find that receiving the order is associated with improved mental health outcomes, particularly for those with personality disorders. However, we also find that the benefits of the order are largely driven by offenders who are not receiving the order due to the court's discretion, and that receiving the order through discretion is associated with worse outcomes.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key identities, and investigate special cases of the generalized Apostol-Hermite polynomials.

Radio maps are two-dimensional representations of wireless signal strength that can be used to create accurate coverage estimates. They have been shown to be particularly useful in scenarios where channel state information is difficult to obtain, such as in the planning of wireless networks. Traditionally, radio map estimation has relied on the collection of signal strength data from various locations using vehicles like lawnmowers or robots. This paper proposes an approach that uses low-cost drones equipped with antennas to create radio maps by flying along pre-planned routes and recording signal strength readings at regularly spaced intervals. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through a comparison with a pattern recognition technique that uses the shapes of recorded signal strength patterns. The results show that the drone-based approach is a reliable option for radio map estimation, particularly in cases where the terrain is constantly changing.

This research introduces a novel anomaly detection technique that leverages Hidden Markov Models (HMM) in an unsupervised learning approach. The method involves training HMMs on time series data under two different conditions: gauge likelihoods that guide the model's parameter optimization and an anomaly-free subset of the data. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through its application to synthetic and real-world datasets.

This study investigates the effectiveness of using audio, visual, and thermal data in person verification systems. We introduce a Multimodal Person Verification System that combines these three modalities and present a novel method for fusing their authentication information. We also introduce the AVT-TBP (Audio-Visual-Thermal-Based Pair Matching) protocol, a two-stage verification process that initially compares person characteristics from similar modalities, and subsequently matches distinctive features across different modalities. We conduct our analysis using the REKFACE dataset, a unique resource that includes thermal face images, and demonstrate the improved accuracy of our system by integrating thermal data, with the authentication rate increasing by 4% compared to a system using only visual and audio data.

Data augmentation is a widely used technique for enhancing model performance by increasing diversity of training data. However, the process is often labor-intensive and difficult to apply to various datasets. This study introduces an unsupervised data augmentation method that requires minimal effort and can be easily adapted to different training sets. The technique uses pre-trained language models to generate new data based on acoustic and transcription similarities. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated by the improvements achieved when applied to the LibriSpeech, MuST-B, and IWSLT datasets.

In a mixture of $k$ distributions, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of the mean of a parameter of interest, denoted as $\theta$. This analysis considers a mixture model where the number of distributions is unknown, but their means can be estimated using a parameter of the model. We derive the asymptotic distribution of this estimator, and propose a Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimator (GMLE) to achieve this. The theoretical findings are illustrated through two practical problems: one involving the estimation of a mixture parameter in a random sampling context, and another related to the Pollock sample size calculation method.

Achieving dependable data privacy has become a pressing concern, particularly when dealing with datasets containing interdependent information. Conventional differential privacy frameworks are ill-equipped to handle this interdependence, leading to significant data degradation. In response, a one-sided differential privacy approach has been developed to maintain dependable privacy for datasets with dependent information. However, this method's effectiveness is contingent on accurate estimates of maximum relative dependencies. In real-world scenarios, determining these dependencies can be challenging. To address this issue, a novel maximum relative dependency estimation framework is proposed, leveraging a distance metric to accurately assess dependencies between data attributes. The proposed method is demonstrated to outperform existing techniques in maximum relative dependency estimation.

The sub-millimeter continuum map of the AS 209 protoplanetary disk by ALMA reveals a notable CO gap at 88 AU. This finding is similar to other disks observed by the MAPS project and is consistent with a dust gap at the same location. We investigate whether the CO gap is caused by gas depletion or chemical alteration using the AS 209 disk as a test case. We analyze CO N=1-0 and C^18O N=1-0 emission from a 0.1" (12 AU) radius area around the dust gap and find that the CO gas is largely depleted. However, C^18O emission is significantly reduced while CO emission shows a noticeable decrease as well. This suggests that CO is more easily depleted than C^18O. We also observe a notable drop in C^18O/CO ratio at the dust gap, indicating the influence of chemical processing. This decrease is consistent with the effects of gas streams and PPD formation. We propose that the CO gap in AS 209 is primarily caused by a combination of gas depletion and chemical alteration.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution and input channels. This paper introduces 'ttree', a highly efficient and adaptable software toolkit for examining time-stamped data, designed to handle large volumes of information with high temporal precision and a large number of input channels. The toolkit is built on top of Python, with a command-line interface and graphical user interface, making it an extremely user-friendly tool. The 'ttree' library is specifically created to facilitate the analysis of data from the CAEN V792N analog-to-digital converter, while also being compatible with other similar devices and formats. The toolkit offers a range of features, including data visualization, event-driven analysis, and customizable computation methods, all of which are highly optimized for speed. This paper provides a detailed overview of the 'ttree' library, along with its implementation, and showcases its capabilities through several practical examples.

We demonstrate existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint on state space, assuming a potential function is concave and uniformly continuous. The approach involves two main steps: first, we establish the existence of solutions with'regular paths'; next, we show these solutions persist under slightly relaxed state constraints.

Recent research identified a group of high-velocity stars moving through our galaxy, linked to a hypothetical structure called a stellar "string". This theoretical framework posits a massive, diffuse object composed of stars, formed when a massive cloud of gas and dust collapsed under its own gravity. However, our re-evaluation of the data suggests an alternative explanation for the observed star movement, focusing on a more traditional, explosive model. This new perspective is supported by the distribution of star velocities and their projected paths, as well as the lack of detectable radio signals from these stars.

The task of visual incompatibility detection, which determines whether an outfit's components are visually compatible, has garnered significant interest in recent times. This research addresses this challenge by developing an innovative framework called VICTOR, which employs a dual transformer architecture to analyze an image and a virtual try-on ensemble created from the individual garment images. The framework's success relies on the use of a fashion-specific contrastive pre-training approach to fine-tune the transformer encoders and a specialized head with multi-layer perceptrons, as well as a loss function that combines BERT and contrastive losses. The model's efficacy is demonstrated through experiments on the Fashionista dataset, where it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving a remarkable 74.4% accuracy after being pre-trained for 20 epochs.

In recent years, quantum information science has shifted its focus from traditional classical and quantum physics to more complex scenarios, exemplified by the increasing interest in quasi-probability distributions such as the Glauber and Wigner functions. These distributions provide a comprehensive framework for describing non-classical photon states, with the Wigner function offering a direct link to the phase-space representation of light. This review aims to provide an in-depth introduction to the rapidly evolving field of generalized quantum phenomena, with a specific focus on the Wigner functions and their applications in optics.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates becomes a significant challenge due to communication constraints. To address this issue, researchers have developed various asynchronous aggregation techniques that enable updates from devices with different update times. These methods buffer incoming gradients and aggregate them from the device that initiated the update, resulting in suboptimal performance compared to synchronous learning. This study introduces a new algorithm, buffered asynchronous aggregation, that enables parallel updates from multiple devices and aggregates gradients from the source with the steepest update, leading to improved convergence rates. Theoretical analysis and empirical experiments demonstrate the benefits of this approach in real-world applications.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We establish this calculus within the polynomial tempered distribution space, thereby expanding the traditional functional calculus application. We also establish a distorted version of this calculus and show it preserves key properties. Furthermore, we examine the inverse operator in the context of a commutative semigroup and derive a distorted functional calculus for a specific class of operators.

The Swampland program's dark energy problem may be resolved through an alternative explanation - that our universe has a hidden dimension. This hypothesis suggests that primordial black holes could constitute a significant portion of dark matter, and their presence in the extra dimension could impact their formation and properties. Assuming a fraction of dark matter composed of these black holes, and that their mass is less than a certain threshold, the existence of a dark radiation component becomes necessary to prevent instability. This, in turn, implies that dark energy's equation of state may not satisfy the required condition, thus presenting an alternative solution to the Swampland program's dark energy conundrum.

The formation of liquid bridges connecting floating objects is a crucial aspect of how objects stuck in a floating raft repel each other. The shape of these liquid bridges determines the forces exerted between the objects. Numerical simulations of breaking liquid bridges reveal the occurrence of two distinct types of failures: one where the bridge collapses under increasing force and another where it fails suddenly without warning. The sudden collapse is made possible by a unique instability that creates a gulf in the bridge, splitting it into separate parts. The shape of these gulf formations is found to be consistent, regardless of the objects' angles of approach or their sizes. The consistency of these gulf shapes holds the key to understanding and predicting the repulsive forces between objects in floating rafts.

We have computationally investigated how anisotropic strain affects the hole mobility in p-type gallium nitride by considering its impact on the in-plane effective mass. Our findings reveal that compressive strain along one axis and tensile strain along the other can significantly lower the in-plane effective mass, thereby increasing the hole mobility. To further optimize this, we have identified two suitable ternary materials, ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$, that can be used to modulate the strain within the GaN lattice.

We've developed a novel approach to robot navigation using a sparse Gaussian process regression model based on temporal difference learning. This model was specifically designed for underwater robots to learn a cost function approximation, facilitating the application of policy search methods in challenging underwater environments. We tested this model in two diverse underwater scenarios and compared its performance to a traditional state-of-the-art model, achieving notable improvements in computation efficiency and data storage for the Gaussian process model, while resulting in a slight performance decrease of about 10%.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a residue. This property enables us to extend the Darboux and Calapso transformations to such surfaces with a meromorphic component.

This study introduces a novel nonparametric method to approximate conditional expectation operators within the context of dynamical systems. It leverages kernel-based techniques and yields a smooth, conditional expectation operator that can be efficiently computed. The method's convergence properties are rigorously established and its practical effectiveness is illustrated through a numerical example.

This paper presents and proves several identities related to $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. Specifically, it explores $\lambda$-analogues of the core-enlarging formula and the substitution formula for $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind.

Temporal knowledge graphs capture complex relationships between entities across various time periods. Link prediction in such graphs presents a challenging task due to the constraints imposed by time. Current approaches that combine static models with attention-based mechanisms for link prediction in temporal graphs have shown some success but have several limitations, including high computational complexity and the inability to handle multiple possible time periods for relationships. To address these issues, we have developed a new method that combines static models with a novel attentional technique, allowing for more efficient and effective link prediction in temporal graphs.

This study delves into the concept of strong shift equivalence for infinite path-finite graphs and its associated C*-algebras, particularly for those of finite source. We demonstrate that the strong shift equivalence relation is equivalent to K-theory equivalence for unital C*-algebras, while also showing that it is an equivalence relation that preserves surjections for graphs and C*-algebras. Additionally, we establish a characterization of strong shift equivalence for graphs through a gauge-invariant approach, which enables the extension of established classification theorems and non-decomposability criteria to the realm of strong shift equivalence.

The heavy quark potential is examined in detail within a magnetized quark-gluon plasma, taking into account its anisotropic nature. By analyzing the heavy quark dissociation, the study reveals its dependence on the direction of quark movement relative to the magnetic field. The research utilizes hard thermal loop perturbation theory to derive the heavy quark propagator, which is then applied to the Landau-Fokker-Planck equation to obtain the dissociation rate. The findings indicate that the dissociation rate is direction-dependent and can be influenced by the magnetic field direction, quark movement, and quark mass.

To effectively answer questions that require in-depth knowledge, we propose integrating language models with knowledge graph reasoning. A specific enhancement is made to BART, a popular transformer-based language model, by incorporating three additional reasoning modules: search, ranking, and query optimization. The search module enables the model to navigate a knowledge graph, the ranking module helps determine relevant entities and relationships, and the query optimization module enables the model to rephrase questions based on its graph search outcomes. Experimental results demonstrate the improved performance of our BART model-based system, particularly in achieving a MACE score of 0.8444 on QuASAR, outperforming the current best method with a 0.0404 MACE score improvement.

We introduce a simplified construction of high dimensional expanders (HDE) or high dimensional transitive graphs (HDT) using covering spaces of simplicial complexes, offering a more direct approach than existing methods. This results in a new, simplified inductive proof of HDE/HDT existence. Our construction also yields a new, simplified HDE/HDT inductive proof, based on a concept analogous to Zassenhaus' method for integer equivalence.

Recent advancements in language models have made it possible to achieve high performance in zero-shot scenarios using prompts. The effectiveness of prompts is often evaluated using a fixed dataset and model, but it is unclear how well they perform across different datasets and models. We conducted a comprehensive study to compare the performance of various prompts across multiple datasets and achieved better results than existing top-performing prompts on SQuAD and CoQA in GLUE. We also analyzed the characteristics of the most effective prompts in our study.

We compute the $\mathscr{L}$-invariants for motives generated by Steenrod actions, specifically the Artin motive, which corresponds to the integers being mapped onto the Steenrod algebra by the Steenrod squares. The $\mathscr{L}$-invariant of the Artin motive is found to be zero, and this result is further extended to a family of general Artin motives supported on $S^{p,q}$ for all $p,q$ integers greater than zero.

We've developed a deep learning method to identify complex multifrequency microwave (MW) fields that ionize Rydberg atoms. The new approach surpasses traditional spin-motion decoupling techniques in recognizing MW frequencies, even when they're extremely close. The deep learning method is highly versatile and can be applied to recognizing MW fields in three-dimensional Rydberg atom arrays, as well as identifying MW-induced spatial patterns within a single atom.
